Getting Tyre Pressure Right on Tour

Tyre pressure is the most overlooked safety factor in motorcycle touring. Incorrect pressure affects grip, handling, braking distance, fuel economy, and tyre life. A fully loaded touring motorcycle requires higher pressures than an unloaded bike, and many riders forget to adjust when they load up for a tour.

Why Pressure Matters

Under-inflated tyres flex excessively, generating heat that can cause a blowout at speed. They also wear unevenly on the shoulders and reduce fuel economy. Over-inflated tyres reduce the contact patch, compromising grip — especially dangerous in the wet conditions common on British roads. The sweet spot gives maximum grip while preventing overheating.

Finding the Right Pressure

Your motorcycle owner's manual provides pressure recommendations for different loading conditions. Typically you will find three settings:

  • Solo rider, no luggage — The lowest recommended pressure, usually 2.2-2.5 bar front and 2.5-2.9 bar rear.
  • Solo rider with luggage — Slightly higher, typically adding 0.2 bar to the rear tyre to support the extra weight.
  • Rider plus pillion with luggage — The highest setting, often 0.3-0.5 bar above solo pressure, especially at the rear.

Checking Pressure Correctly

Always check tyre pressure when the tyres are cold — before riding or at least two hours after your last ride. Warm tyres show higher pressure due to heat expansion, giving a misleadingly high reading. Check every morning before the day's riding.

Invest in a quality digital pressure gauge. Petrol station gauges are notoriously inaccurate. A dedicated motorcycle gauge costs under twenty pounds and fits easily in your tank bag.

Pressure Monitoring on Tour

Tyre pressure monitoring systems (TPMS) provide real-time pressure readings on your dashboard or phone. Aftermarket TPMS kits from brands like Fobo and TireMoni use valve stem sensors that transmit to a handlebar display or smartphone app. They alert you immediately if pressure drops, potentially saving you from riding on a slowly deflating tyre.

A 10 percent drop in tyre pressure reduces the tyre's load-carrying capacity by approximately 20 percent and increases rolling resistance significantly. On a loaded touring bike, this can mean the difference between a safe tyre and a dangerous one.

Temperature Effects

British temperatures vary significantly between early morning and afternoon, and between seasons. A tyre inflated to 2.5 bar at 20 degrees will read approximately 2.3 bar at 5 degrees. During spring and autumn touring when temperature swings are large, check pressures more frequently to account for these natural variations.
